analysis.one_liner: Gives patients the legal right to control who sees their medical records, with fines and prison terms for violators.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in two House committees for eighteen months, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first comprehensive federal privacy law for medical records. Anyone holding health information — insurers, doctors, employers, schools — would have to get written consent before sharing it, let patients see and correct their own records, keep security safeguards on computerized data, and face civil fines up to $500,000 and criminal penalties up to 10 years for wrongful disclosure. Patients could also sue violators directly. The bill was introduced in June 1997, referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never acted on again.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients. Today, health information can be shared with many people who have no role in a person's care, often without the person's knowledge or consent, and federal privacy protection is minimal while state rules vary widely [S3]. The bill would give every individual the right to inspect and copy their own records, correct errors, receive written notice of how their information is used, and sue violators for damages — including $25,000 liquidated damages for a material violation and $50,000 when the violation was willful or done for profit, plus attorney's fees [S3]. It would also bar employers from making a job conditional on a broad release of health records [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and anyone with medical records

how_it_helps.text: Every holder of health information would need the patient's written, purpose-specific, revocable authorization before disclosing records, and could disclose only the minimum information necessary for the purpose [S3].
Individuals would gain the right to inspect and copy their records within 30 days, request corrections within 45 days, and be notified of an organization's information practices [S3].

Repeat violators would face civil penalties up to $500,000 and exclusion from Medicare, Medicaid, and other federally funded health programs, and knowing disclosure for commercial gain could bring up to 10 years in prison [S3].
Patients could sue directly for injunctive relief, actual or liquidated damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees — a remedy federal law currently lacks [S3].
Stronger state privacy laws would not be preempted, and Social Security numbers could not be used to link or identify health records [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans, insurers, health care providers, employers, schools, and data companies that hold health information would bear the cost of written authorizations, security safeguards, audit trails, disclosure accounting, and potential fines — up to $25,000 per violation and $500,000 for a pattern of violations, or exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid [S3]. Law enforcement would face a higher bar for obtaining medical records, including notice and a right for the individual to challenge warrants in court [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be expensive: holders of health records would need written authorizations on separate forms, administrative and electronic security safeguards, seven-year records of disclosures, and audit trails for every electronic access attempt — a heavy burden, especially for small medical practices [S3].

The bill would sharply restrict law enforcement access to medical records: police would need clear and convincing evidence that records are necessary, warrant executions would be minimally examined and sealed, and individuals would get notice and 15 days to challenge a warrant in court — requirements prosecutors would argue hamper legitimate investigations [S3].

Penalties are severe and run against a wide range of actors — including employers and schools — and a violation 'general business practice' could mean exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid, a sanction that could end a business [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: as its own findings state, there was little federal protection for the confidentiality of health information, protection varied greatly from state to state, and computerization and genetic testing were creating new ways for sensitive records to spread without consent [S3]. The main costs were compliance paperwork and reduced convenience for police and researchers — researchers could still obtain coded or nonidentifiable data through institutional review boards without individual authorization [S3]. The design was strict but coherent: it carved out exceptions for emergencies, public health, oversight, accreditation, and judicial proceedings [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and forwarded to subcommittees the following week, but neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott and nine original cosponsors introduced the bill on June 5, 1997 [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee [S5].
On June 16 it was sent to the Government Management, Information and Technology Subcommittee, and on June 18 to the Health and Environment Subcommittee [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a markup, a hearing, a floor vote, or Senate consideration, and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that hold, buy, and sell Americans' health records — insurers, employers, and medical data brokers — were better off, because no comprehensive federal privacy rule was enacted and their access to health information stayed largely unregulated for the rest of the decade.

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its advocacy as a physician-legislator focused on medical privacy.

for.name: 21 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 21 listed cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support.

against.name: Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 5, 1997 and never brought the bill before the committee or reported it out; the record shows no action beyond subcommittee referral.

against.name: Dan Burton
against.role: Chair, House Government Reform and Oversight Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the second referral the same day; the bill was sent to a subcommittee on June 16 and never acted on again.

against.name: Health insurers and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive federal medical privacy legislation during the late-1990s debate, favoring voluntary industry standards over enforceable restrictions and penalties.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 21 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the two Republican-chaired committees to which it was referred never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar plans from conditioning coverage or payment on broad record releases, limit disclosures to the minimum necessary, and expose repeat violators to $500,000 fines and exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid. Patients' records could no longer flow freely to affiliates and marketers.

industries.industry: Medical data brokers and insurance support organizations
industries.note: Companies that assemble and sell health information to insurers would become regulated trustees, barred from aggregating or matching records across organizations without specific patient authorization.
Employers would be prohibited from conditioning employment on authorizations for record disclosure and from linking or matching an employee's health records held by different organizations.

Providers would carry significant compliance costs for authorizations, safeguards, and audit trails, but the bill's own findings argue that assured confidentiality keeps patients from avoiding care, and provider information would be protected to preserve service availability.

Police and prosecutors would need clear and convincing evidence that records are necessary, and individuals would get notice of warrant executions and a right to challenge them in court — a far higher bar than existing practice.
